idiom_name: Proxy membrane behind an interface-typed facade (ProxyHandler<T>)
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the same engine and uses the same primitive: a Proxy with a handler typed ProxyHandler<T> mediates the calls, and the facade is declared as the interface type so consumers keep static checking. The type system stops at the membrane, though: trap return types are unconstrained, so nothing checks that the wrapper's behaviour matches the declared interface and the unavoidable cast (`new Proxy(target, handler) as T`) is where the guarantee lives - in the handler, not in the types. Where the mediated surface is a small fixed interface, a hand-written class implementing that interface and forwarding per method keeps the compiler honest and is often preferred; the Proxy route pays off when the wrapped object is dynamic or the interface is large and evolving. Either way the identity map and revocation are hand-written, exactly as in JavaScript.
pitfalls: The `as T` cast is unavoidable and unchecked: TypeScript cannot see that a trap returned the wrong shape, so conformance of the membrane to its interface is a runtime property, not a compile-time one.

Proxies do not forward private fields: a proxied instance has a different identity and no access to the original object's #private elements, so classes with private state cannot be wrapped transparently (MDN).
Declaring the facade as the interface leaks nothing at runtime: consumers who use the wrapped object as a Map key or compare identity need the identity-map wrapper factory, not a fresh Proxy.
Structural typing accepts any object with the right shape as the target, so a partially-implemented wrapper type-checks; the policy, not the signature, must state which members are mediated.
